content: The antiviral activity of zidovudine against HIV-1 has been evaluated in various cell lines, including monocytes and freshly isolated human peripheral blood lymphocytes. The effective concentration range for zidovudine was determined to be between 1 and 9 μM. In studies conducted by Monogram Biosciences, baseline samples from 135 subjects in the ESS30009 study showed a median effective concentration (EC50) of 0.034 μM. In cell culture drug combination studies, zidovudine exhibited synergistic activity when combined with nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) such as abacavir, didanosine, and lamivudine; non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) such as delavirdine and nevirapine; and protease inhibitors including indinavir, nelfinavir, ritonavir, and saquinavir. Zidovudine also demonstrated additive activity when combined with interferon alfa. However, ribavirin was found to inhibit the phosphorylation of zidovudine in cell culture. Genotypic analyses of HIV-1 isolates selected in cell culture and recovered from zidovudine-treated patients revealed mutations in the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) gene. These mutations resulted in six amino acid substitutions: M41L, D67N, K70R, L210W, T215Y or T215F, and K219Q, which confer resistance to zidovudine. Higher levels of resistance were associated with a greater number of these amino acid substitutions. In some patients harboring zidovudine-resistant virus at baseline, phenotypic sensitivity to zidovudine was restored after 12 weeks of combination therapy with lamivudine and zidovudine. Furthermore, combination therapy with lamivudine and zidovudine delayed the emergence of resistance-associated substitutions to zidovudine. In a study involving 167 HIV-1-infected patients, isolates with multi-drug resistance to didanosine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine, and zidovudine were recovered from patients treated for one year or longer with zidovudine plus didanosine or zidovudine plus zalcitabine. The resistance-associated amino acid substitution patterns observed with these combination therapies (A62V, V75I, F77L, F116Y, Q151M) differed from those seen with zidovudine monotherapy. Among these, the Q151M substitution was most commonly associated with multi-drug resistance. The substitution at codon 151, in combination with substitutions at codons 62, 75, 77, and 116, resulted in a virus with reduced susceptibility to didanosine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine, and zidovudine. Thymidine analogue mutations (TAMs), which are selected by zidovudine, confer cross-resistance to other antiretroviral agents, including abacavir, didanosine, stavudine, tenofovir, and zalcitabine.
